The story of Peterson's death was told in Stratford today by Mrs. James Biereholm, whose husband and brother-in-law were members of the fishing party of Saturday, which ended fatally for Peterson.

DETROIT, Mich. July 31.—Sam Crawford, the big Tiger outfielder and one of the most popular ball players who ever wore a Detroit uniform, has decided to resist the temptation of running for sheriff on the Democratic ticket. Local Democrats figure that the wide popularity of "Wahoo Sam" with the fans of the city would result in his rolling up a winning vote; have pleaded hard with him to allow them to make him a candidate.

WASHINGTON, July 5.—Early resumption of friendly diplomatic conversations with the de facto government of Mexico to the end that peace and order may be restored in northern Mexico and along the border is expected here to be the next step of the United States in its relations with its southern neighbor.

The crisis precipitated by Villa's raid on Columbus, N.M., and culminating in the fight at Carrizal, Mexico, between American and Mexican troops appeared tonight to have been dissipated by an amicable note from General Carranza presented during the day by his ambassador designate here, Eliseo Arredondo. The note proposes that the differences between the governments be settled by mediation or by direct negotiations. It is remarkable for its brevity, its restrained and friendly tone and for the absolute lack of any of the strong, even insolent language which characterized the last two communications from the de facto government. It treats as closed incident the exchange of unfriendly communications which brought war almost within sight.

No formal comment on the note was obtainable from the State Department officials. A copy was forwarded to the White House immediately on its receipt and President WILSON will determine on the course to be pursued. The fact that Secretary Lansing completed preparations today for a month's vacation to begin Friday is regarded as significant, however, of a feeling on his part that the crisis is over.

Favors Mediation.

As matter of general principle the Washington government always has favored mediation of any dispute suitable for such procedure. There is every indication, however, that in the present instance it will be deemed desirable to conduct forthcoming negotiations directly with the Carranza government.

Diplomatic corps here are expected to make inquiry soon as to the attitude of the Washington government in view of the statement of the Mexican foreign office that it awaits only a decision here as to whether mediation or direct negotiations would be preferable. Indications tonight were that the inquiries would be met with assurances that the two governments had reached a stage where they would not find it necessary to call upon the friendly services of their neighbor states.

It is not known whether a formal reply to General Carranza's note is contemplated. Diplomatic usage does not call for one, and many officials feel that more can be accomplished through informal discussion between Mr. Arredondo and Counsellor POLK who will act as secretary in Mr. Lansing's absence, than could be hoped for in any other way. It is understood Mr. Arredondo plans to call at the department tomorrow to say good-by to Secretary Lansing on his departure for his vacation. Probably the preliminary steps necessary for the inauguration of the informal discussion will be taken then. State Department officials appeared entirely satisfied with the definition of the matters to be settled outlined in the new Mexican note. It is presented in this language as translated in the embassy:

There Are Two Problems.

"The American government believes, reasonably, that the insecurity of its frontier is a source of difficulty and the Mexican government on its part believes that the stay of American troops on Mexican territory, aside from being a trespass on the sovereignty of Mexico, is the immediate cause of the conflicts. Therefore, the withdrawal of American troops on the one hand and the protection of the frontier on the other are the two essential problems, the solution of which must be the directing or order of the efforts of both governments."

Coupled with this definition is an outline of a sort of military status quo beyond the border which the de facto government suggests as substitute for its previous demands for immediate withdrawal of the American troops. It is stated as follows:

At the same time it hopes that the American government on its part may make use of all effort to prevent also new acts of its military and civil authorities of the frontier that might cause new complications."

"Clean Up by May Day" is the mes
sage of the Civics Committee of the
Ohio Federation of Women's Clubs
to the club women throughout the
state. Let May Day, 1916, be cele-
brated in every community by civic
regeneration and new civic spirit
stimulated by community cooperation
for community betterment during the
month of April. Every community
will be greatly benefited by such
course.


If the women of Ohio will cooperate
in the general movement the cam
paign will not only be vigorous, but
itation, better homes, cleaner streets,
finer gardens, Fairgrounds and parks,
less fire loss and lower fire insurance
rates. The -women's clubs of Ohio
have undertaken to do their share in
this matter In fact they are leading
In the movement.


When the housewife dons her apron
and prepares to clean the house the
mere male citizen usually takes to the
street. If he does take to the street
this spring he will find that the house
wife has been before him and that
cleanup activities are being prose
cuted Just as vigorously there as in
the house. If he goes to his club he
will find the same condition. If he
goes to his Office he will find the jani-
tor service augmented and that a
rapid elimination Of accum dlated dust
and dirt is going on. Hurriedly pass
ing into the street as he once more
starts to dodge a general cleanup,
he will find activity on every side
which betokens a people aroused and
g determination to make things clean
and keep them so. Battered buildings,
known for years as fire-traps, will. be
razed, old houses and buildings will be
repainted, repairs will be carried on
everywhere, and on vacant lots where
weeds, well nourished by tin cans and
refuse, formerly grew to forest height,
he will find school boys and girls bus
lily planting flowers and trees.


And yet if the plans of the Civics
Committee of Ohio Federation of
Women's Clubs are carried out, all
this will be done without confusion and
without placing too great tax upon
the city's facilities for handling dirt.
1t is proposed to stretch the campaign
this year over the entire month Of
April, and when this is done to follow
up the work and keep these places
clean and beautiful. The man who
this spring observes unwonted activ-
ity in the way of cleaning and paint
ing, will be amazed at the marvellous
contrast with former conditions, and
he will never witness the same thing
again. This campaign will be con-
tinuous. In future years there will be
spring clean-ups, but none which will
produce the accumulation of rubbish
shown by the campaign in 1915. In
Cincinnati, where two systematic cam
paigns have been held, the results
achieved by the second campaign were
not nearly so important as those OF
the first. The work was we'll done in
The first place, and active committees
aided by the municipal officers kept
things pretty clean throughout the
year.


We need more attention to the
cleanliness, order and beauty of our
environment Likewise we need to
realize that our surroundings are to
a very large extent what we ourselves
make them.


Is it not worth while to make Ohio
state of beautiful towns and vii
lagos? The influence on the character

what the young cotton will do yet.

about equally divided between young
and old cotton.

Special Correspondent.

New London, Conn. Sept 6.—Assurance that the Constitutionalist government de facto now possesses the military strength necessary completely TO control all the Northern states of the Republic and put an end TO border raids on American life and property was given to-day by the Carranza envoys at the first formal conference of the American-Mexican joint commission at the Griswold Hotel.

Following exchange of credentials the conference spent three hours reviewing the history and development of the Carranza revolution and administration. Luis Cabrera, chairman of the Mexican division, presided and took the lead in describing the gradual rise to power of the Constitutionalists. He declared that most substantial progress had been made not only in military affairs, but in the social and economic status of the country also.

The task of restoring order, commerce and industry, he asserted, had been prosecuted with the utmost sincerity and perseverance and notable success had been achieved during the last two years and especially since the recognition of Carranza by the United States.

Railroad Work Outlined.

Commissioner Alberto J. FAM, who is president of the National Railways of Mexico, outlined the accomplishments of his government in reopening 10,000 miles of railroad. Practically all lines, the American Commissioners were told, are now in operation, the resumption of normal traffic on some roads being hindered only by shortage of equipment and need of repairs.

It is understood that Mexico's need of an immediate gold loan of from 50,000,000 to 100,000,000 has been impressed upon the American Commissioners. Reconstruction in Mexico, authorities are agreed, will call for an expenditure of at least $50,000,000 and will mean the practical rebuilding of about 10,000 miles of track and the purchase of a large amount of rolling stock and other equipment.

The Constitutionalist government has announced that it intends, within a short time, to restore all commandeered railroads to their owners in the same physical and financial condition as when they were taken over by the revolutionary forces in 1910. To effect this alone a large extension of credit would be required and those in close touch with the Mexican mediators say that American cooperation in the problem of funds will be urged upon the conference as imperative as soon as the border question has been settled.

Adjourn Until Friday.

Following the conference to-day, the commissioners sent telegrams to President Wilson and General Carranza expressing the hope that success would crown their labors here. They then adjourned until Friday morning, Commissioner Cabrera explaining that sudden summons to Boston would prevent his presence here to-morrow. Secretary Lane, chairman of the American division, said the day would be devoted to revision of the subjects considered to-day and the collection of data.

A two hours excursion of President Wilson's yacht, the Mayflower, this afternoon relieved the tedium of diplomatic debate. To the accompaniment of Mexican airs, played by the President's band, the yacht, with the mediators and families aboard, left New London at 3 o'clock, and steamed twenty miles toward the open sea. Soon after rounding Eastern Point the Mayflower was enveloped in thick fog which, except for brief intervals, lasted throughout the trip. Frequent soundings were made by the commander to determine his position.

"That's how we must find our way out of the fog which surrounds Mexico," said one of the commission attaches; "by sounding the uncharted depths of super-diplomacy, and hoping to reach terra firma, though not to be landed high and dry."

time decrease in plant food. In fact,

Intensive tillage, deep plowing, thorough

Fertilizers often enable crops to
take out more potash, phosphorus, and
nitrogen, particularly nitrogen, than the
fertilizers themselves contain. They
may increase production, but decrease
total plant food.

Two tons of limestone should be ap-
plied to the majority of acres in Ten-
nessee. It places potash and phos-
phorus in reach of plants, but it adds
none to the soil. It does not even add
nitrogen, unless legumes are intro-
duced to the cropping system to be
plowed under or fed and the manure
returned to the land.

lage, fertilizers, lime—all have a place
in soil-building. Making plant food
available is the farmer's business. So
is making soils durable and perma-
nent. Worn soils are the natural re-
sults of placing fertility in reach only
of soil-robbing crops—grains, corn,
cotton, tobacco, etc. Soil-building crops
have not received their share of the
benefits.

It is a necessary thing to make
plant foods available by all possible
agencies, but they should be directed
first toward the increased production

On the next rush Legore fumbled as he was tackled, the pigskin bounding toward the Crimson goal until Gates caught it up and ran to the 12- yard mark.

 While the Yale stands called for a touchdown and the Harvard supporters begged the Crimson to hold, Harvard was forced back, foot by foot, four downs gaining the necessary 10 yards. With two yards needed, Yale crashed three times into the Harvard defense for slight gains and then Neville slid over the backs of the low playing Crimson scrimmagers for the touchdown that won the game, the first made by the Blue against Harvard since Captain Ted Coy crossed the Crirn- son line at Cambridge in 1907.

 JONES' SYSTEM WINS

 Two years later, the same Coy kicked two field goals against Harvard, thus winning the last victory for the Blue un- til today's conquest. Tad Jones, whose coaching system triumphed over that of Haughtons, was a prominent factor in that victory.

 Early Harvard showed the smooth ma chine-like play for which recent Crimson teams have been noted. but under the terrific attack of the powerful Yale line the forwards broke badly and the back field found it difficult to get under way. When Yale had the ball the Harvard line could not hold the Eli rushes and the defense was constantly called upon.

 A heavy field made the brilliant runs Of Casey and Legore difficult and both slipped and fell several times when they were just swinging into their stride. Hor- weens bunting was superior to that of Neville and Legore, but there was little choice in the play and tackling of the end pairs, which was the best exhibi- ton seen on eastern fields this season. The play of the Yale line, from tackle to tackle, was better than that of liar wards.

 STATISTICS FAVOR ELI

 Statistics show clearly the extent of Yale's superiority. The Blue team gained first down seven times to Harvard's five. not speak the words. A look told her
husband to do it for her.


"You are going away with me, Rob-
bie," he said.


"When am I coming back?"


There was an ominous silence.


"I'm not going away," said the boy,
refusing to put his arms in the sleeves
of his coat. His sister went to him,
threw her arms about him and, look-
ing up at her father, said:


"You shan't take Robbie away!"


The mother gently tried to separate
the children, but they clung to each
other and to her. She looked with a roseate
appeal to her husband for help.


"Come, come, little girl," he said,
laying his hand on the soft little arm.
But she only clung the tighter to her
brother and her mother.


"Papa," said the boy, "take mamma
and Ethel, and I'll go with you."


"No, no," said the girl; "you and
papa stay here with mamma and me."


Seizing her father's hand, she tried
to put it round herself, her brother and
her mother. The boy, seeing what she
was endeavoring to do, caught his
mother's hand and tried to do the
same. The mother looked at the fa-
ther. The eyes of both were wet.
Then the father arose and beckoned
his wife to join him in another room.


"Sweetheart," he said and paused.
The words he would speak were chok-
ing in his throat. Finally he found
voice to go on: "Give me another trial.
I was—well, crazy, to talk to you as
I did. Forgive me—I think I can go
forever without—"


He could not bear to designate the
brutality of what he had said.


She covered her face with her hands;
he went to her and put his arms about
her.


"For their sake, for yours, promise
that I will never again lose my self-
control."


"I will try to bear with you as you
bear with me—" she moaned. "For
their sakes perhaps we can—


I—we must."


When they left the room the father
went down and dismissed the carriage
at the door, while the mother went to
the children.


"Papa and Robbie are not going
away," she said, kissing them.


The children clapped their hands and
danced about the room.


That was their last violent quarrel.
Both placed guard upon their tongues
and when the choler rose recalled the
scene of their former intended parting.
Meanwhile marital association as well
as the children was drawing them
closer together.

Christian people who were converted in the past but who had gradually grown cold reconsecrated themselves to the cause of Jesus Christ and the active workers received new inspiration for future service in the conversion of so many of their friends and classmates.

Plans have been laid for weekly prayer meetings and daily devotional groups. The Department owes great to the Rev. Mr. Knight for the great sermons he has delivered and to God for the blessings which He has given it.

We girls of the College Department feel that we too have received a large portion of the blessings of the past week. We have had the great joy of seeing six of our dedicate their lives to the Christ. Chicago, ILL.,, Sept. 25.-Boston today
still maintains its lead of two and one
half games over Chicago with Detroit
one-half a game behind Chicago in
the contest for the American league
championship. All three leaders won
their games Friday and there was no
change in the relative standing.


In the National league Brooklyn is
entrenched in first place, two and one
half games in front of Philadelphia
and five and a half games ahead of
Boston. Brooklyn and Philadelphia
each have thirteen games to play and
Boston has seventeen.


Braves Out.


A sudden reversal of form, sustained
while Matty'S Reds were visiting Bean
Town, has placed the Braves so far
down in the list that nothing short of
an epidemic of infantile paralysis or
broken legs in the Dodger and Phil
adelphia teams will put the Braves in
the lead.


The Stallings bunch now is five and
half games behind the pace-setting
Dodgers and three games behind Phil
adelphia-a margin which it is I'M
possible to overcome in the remaining
sixteen ga-leS the Braves can play
! Gradually the Red Sox are pound
| ing their way to the American league
pennant. They did not, gain on Chi
cago and Detroit in their game Frida y
for the two runners-up also won. But
they brought their schedule one game
nearer completion and if they win
seven more games of their remaining
ten, it will be impossible for Chicago
to overtake them.


Giants ClimbiI =.
The Braves, besides being forced to
watch Cincinnati knock the props
from under their pennant hopes, now
are seriously threatened by the Giants,
who won their seventeenth straight
game and are bidding strong for third
place.


The Giants now stand three games
and one point behind the Braves and
have sixteen games to play If they
can keep up their great work they
will pass the Braves, for they still have
series with the Braves. The Braves
also must meet Philadelphia, their last
series of the season.


The Dodgers hold two and a half
game lead over the Phillies since their
parting wallop at the Cardinals yes
terday and they began today against
the Cubs, a team which isn't expected
to make it overly interesting for the
leaders. Philadelphia is billed with
the Reds and in view of the way the
Reds attacked the Braves, it must be
conceded they are due to a least make
it interesting for the second place
team.

Until a year or two ago, the use of motor cars was largely restricted to warm weather use. Most people bought them for pleasure, rather than utility and immediately Jack Frost waved his icy hand, they promptly garaged them and allowed them to rust until nature turned green again. The demand started with those who felt that an investment in two cars—open and closed—was worth to them the expenditure involved. The limousine, the berline, and the landaulet obviously added much to the joy and ease of living and caused the average American to think seriously of a winter conveyance of his own.

Then came closed bodies to be interchanged on the same chassis with open touring or roadster bodies. This reduced somewhat the cost of inter-season driving, but the initial investment and expense of changing bodies twice a year was still greater than

The idea of a simple, demountable top that could be handled by two or three inexpert men, not so worked out that it would not suffer in looks when compared to a full closed body occurred to me three years ago. Unfortunately the type of touring car then prevailing did not lend itself readily to the plan.

The accepted open car had four doors and two compartments, the driver and his companion sitting absolutely apart from those in the rear of the tonneau. To put a top on such a car meant a make-shift appearance not at all acceptable to persons of taste and refinement.

Plainly the thing to do was to first popularize a new type of open car and this I set out to do. Our body department designed a touring car with divided front seats and only two entrance doors, the latter being very wide and located on either side in the rear. We built two sample models and quietly introduced them at the New York and Chicago shows in 1914.

This new touring car became immediately popular, orders for them at the shows being so many that we decided to make the model standard. This we did in the early spring of 1914 and it was the conspicuously successful novelty of the season. The divided front seat was soon adopted by nearly all leading manufacturers.

The way was then clear to carry out our plans for the all-year car that we had had so long in mind. We announced the all-year car in August 1914, and there was never from the start the slightest doubt of its acceptance. The interest was everywhere—east, west, north and south. In fact it was so much greater than we had anticipated that we found necessary to forthwith increase the capacity of our body factory.

Our all-year car was exhibited at the national shows for the first time last year and was then still without competition. But the handwriting was on the wall, other makers realized it plainly and this year witnesses twenty or more demountable tops of various kinds on the market.

The triumph of the two-in-one convertible car is one of the greatest booms to the motor car industry in its whole history. It has boosted winter sales to proportions never before thought possible. And to the people it has brought the advantages of winter driving at little more expense than that involved in the ownership of an open car alone.

ions and they followed him out of
the room.


Then the door was shut again,
bolts shot home and the key was
turned in the lock. I was alone,
should be left alone probably until
near noon tomorrow. Then Fa-
ther Anthony might come to help
me make my peace with Heaven.


My labors, worthy or not, were
over, finished. There was no
more need to scheme and plan.
I could be idle and dream. Tomor-
row—tomorrow at noon. I must
have slipped low in the chair as
sleep overcame me, for my next
conscious effort was in struggling
to drag myself out of some deep
hole into which I had fallen,
while a voice was urging me to
hurry.


"Quickly! Quickly!"


I staggered to my feet. Stand-
ing before me was the little kitch-
en-maid.


"Come, sir, come. Every mo-
ment counts tonight."


I only awoke thoroughly as
I followed her across the room, to
a corner of it hung with tapestry,
but now it was flung aside and
showed that a piece of stonework
was missing. The hole I looked
into was black, uninviting as a
vault.


"There is light below" said
the child. "The ladder is on this
side; your foot will touch the top
of it at once. Go first. I must
follow because I know how to
close the trap."


Without a word I put my foot
upon the ladder which was
clamped perpendicularly to the
wall and went down slowly. A
miracle had happened. There
had opened for me a way of
escape.

Calling out the guard for the time and the present military law brings up the fact that as written the act authorizes the President to use the state soldiers either within or without the United States territory.

The provision authorizing the use of the guardsmen as such beyond the border was held to be unconstitutional by former Attorney General Wickersham. It never has been passed upon by the Supreme Court, however, and President Wilson has full legal authority to employ the state forces beyond the border if he so desires. Only an injunction against the War Department could prevent it.

By the terms of the law the guardsmen must be mustered into the service of the United States before they come under separate control of the federal government. The full enrolled strength of each regiment called out is liable for service under penalty of courtmartial.

Army officers believe there will be no difficulty in getting out the full strength. They anticipate instead the support of the enlistment in the National Guard of the three states, because of the chance for active service.

President Wilson specified no time of service in his call. The law authorizes him to do so but does not make it mandatory. The situation is such that no forecast as to time can be made.

Eliseo Arredondo, Mexican ambassador designate, at the State Department today formally repudiated in the name of his government alarming statements that General Obregon had presented a demand for immediate withdrawal of the American troops in Mexico.

Mr. Arredondo's statement was telegraphed to General Funston for his information in meeting the situation on the border. New York, Dec. 1.—Can money went up or rather was marked up to 1 per cent and the Industrial list, after a strong beginning, broke to points with losses of a point to 2 points and 2 half in the rails. This in brief is the story of to-day's market.


Nobody of any experience in Wall Street affairs would attempt to maintain that this fury in call loans was due to natural causes. The surplus of the New York banks has, to be sure, been coming down rapidly for the last month and a half and the $10,000,000 reported on Saturday was the lowest in the history of the clearing house under the new regime. But even a $200,000,000 surplus reserve at this season of the year when in the past deficits have been frequent certainly does not imply any scarcity of funds.


The significant thing today was that time money did not advance with call loans. Had there been a real deficiency in the money supply it would have affected all maturities and not simply demand loans. The whole truth was that the jump to 1 per cent in the call rate was engineered by the banks at the instigation of powerful interests which have been heavy sellers during the last week or so on the floor of the stock exchange. Distribution had been carried far enough for those on the inside to desire a shake-out and the money market was the instrument used to produce the desired result. This bit of manipulation had to be tried just when it was because after the gold now on its way from the Pacific coast and from Canada reaches New York it would be hard to bring about such an upturn as was witnessed today.


It is needless to say that the market is in a very much better position as a result of this setback.

Among the industrials Anaconda was heavily sold on its November production figures showing a large decrease as compared with both October and September.

The Federal Farm Loan Act. popularly called the rural credits law was signed by the president and became a law on July II. The primary purpose of this act is to promote agricultural prosperity by enabling farmers to borrow money on farm mortgage security at a reasonable rate of interest and for relatively long periods of time. To attain this object two farm mortgage systems are provided: first, a system operating through regional land banks and second, a system operating through joint stock land banks.

To attract money to the farm loan field the act provides a method whereby those who have money to lend can find safe investments in the form of debentures or bonds of small and large denominations issued by the banks and based on the security of mortgages on farm lands.

These two systems are to be under the general supervision of a Federal Farm Loan Board in the Treasury Department, composed of the Secretary of the Treasury as chairman ex officio and four members appointed by the President. This board has authority to appoint appraisers, examiners and registrars, who will be public officials.

The Federal Land Bank system

Under the Federal Land Bank system is set provided for Federal land banks, which make loans for the first twelve months exclusively through local mortgage farm loan associations composed of borrowers. These associations shall be shareholders in the banks and in this act members who are borrowers will share in the profits of the bank. The money for the loans is to come partly from the capital of the banks and partly from the sale by the banks of bonds.

Robber Robbed and Recovered Money.

In reply to a telegram from Armoge friends, J. T. Palmer, cashier at the First State Bank at Tuskalusa, Okla., gives the details of the robbery of his bank and of the capture of the robber. The letter follows.

Tuskalusa, Okla., Jan. 11, 1916.
Spreads, Scott & Lacy,
Armoge, Oklahoma

DEAR BRETHREN,

Your telegram received and I will in this way tell you just how it happened. The bank building is of brick with large windows on each side that raise easily, screen wire on windows. Building 30x40 feet, fixtures with glass instead of wood, top vault at back, safe in front window.

It was a cold day and this young fellow, a small man about like Lacy, had been standing around the stove in the lobby most of the day and had kept my eye on him, as he acted rather peculiarly. In the afternoon he came in about 2:00 and took his usual position by the stove, his old rubber coat got hot and was smelling rather loud and I said, "Partner you are liable to burn your coat." He made some remark and said he was cold. We had very few customers that afternoon, and I had just balanced up my cash and stacked it—put some cash items with the currency under a rubber band and placed it on the tray of silver and some gold, and carried it to the safe and set it in the window, opened the safe and was winding the timer. I heard him make three quick steps and peck on the glass—I knew what was up and did not look around for a second. He said, "Hey there, hold up." I said, "What's the matter with YOU?" and looked around and asked him what he wanted and beheld two large German automatic pistols pointing at me. He grinned and said, "I want your money." I said, "All right, come and get it, but be careful with your guns, if you hurt me you won't get a cent." He motioned me back towards the door that enters the office. When he came in, he punched me in the belly with one of his guns, and I again cautioned him about the careless manner he was handling the artillery. He handed me the sack and told me to put the money in it. I told him to come to the safe and get it. He followed. The Capt. did not catch on at once until I asked the robber if he wanted the silver, then the Capt. ducked and jumped out at the front door. I ran around the bank and made for his gun, the robber attempted to shoot, but the Captain was too quick for him. I placed my hand under the gun and asked him not to shoot. United Press Services


NEW YORK, Feb. 1. I.—Throughout the United States, beginning today, the Young Women's Christian Asso. jubilee starts its national public month celebrating the fiftieth anniversary of the founding of the association in Boston, March 3, 1866.


Nine hundred and sixty-six associations, including city, county and student, have developed and exist today as the result of that first association, which was started by a society of women to help needy, supporting girls who came to the city to seek employment. The organization membership in America today numbers 32,956. The association owns millions of dollars worth of property in buildings, to which hundreds of thousands of young women go for education, recreation, to make friends and to find a place to live. Beginning with a nation-wide membership rally today, the jubilee month will be filled with celebrations and events.


February 9 and 11 will be pioneer days, on which every member of the organization, past and present, will report back to the local association which was her first interest. On February 22d the historical pageant, "Girls of Yesterday and Today" will be presented in every association building in the country. This will be a four-act play in which the girl of 1866 and the girl of 1915 will interpret through the medium of the other members of the company, the scenes that pass before them. There are only two speaking parts in the pageant. On March 3d will be celebrated the fiftieth anniversary of the association's work in America.

and the most dignified course now

New York, Nov. 22.—The campaign to obtain $2,100,000 for the new Federation for the Support of Jewish Philanthropic societies is acquiring greater momentum every day through the addition of new workers for the cause. Not only are business men and social workers doing their utmost, but the women's plans for the campaign are being furthered along interesting lines.

Three prominent women—Mrs. Jacob H. Schiff, Mrs. Daniel Guggenheim and Mrs. William B. Einstein—threw open their homes yesterday afternoon for meetings of volunteer women workers and to obtain pledges for the federation.

Under the leadership of Mrs. Emil Baerwald, young Jewish women have organized luncheons and afternoon teas and are soliciting funds for charity. Mrs. Baerwald has eight committees at work, composed mainly of young women. In addition to the actual labor of gathering pledges, said Mrs. Baerwald, many of her aids were dipping into their allowances to make contributions to the federation. "We are getting our money in small amounts," said Mrs. Baerwald. "Some of it is coming from girls who work for a living. Teachers, workers in settlement houses and members of girls' working clubs are giving according to their means."

The young women are canvassing the entire city. The work is so divided up that everything is done in a systematic way. There is a committee, headed by Mrs. Joseph C. Dreyfus, working among East Side organizations, such as the Educational Alliance, day nurseries and settlement houses. Among the Young Women's Hebrew Association branches Miss Henrietta Guggenheim's committee is conducting an energetic campaign. The younger members of the synagogues are being interested in aiding the federation through a committee headed by Miss Lucille Martin. There is a college and working girls committee, the chairman of which is Miss Marianne Breuer.

The aim of the new federation is to coordinate the various Jewish philanthropic activities to avoid unnecessary duplication of activities and to prevent waste. Felix M. Waxburg is president.

Mount Wolf, Pa, April S.-York
county is not trailing along on the
wave of prosperity which is sweeping
over the country at the present time.
She is among the leaders, and is one of
the busiest sections in the State.
Goldsboro and York Haven are rushed
with work, the result of the big war
in Europe, and now come the reports
from Cmigsville and Mount Wolf
which show that those towns are in
very f1ourishing conditions.


Both OF these towns are attractive
to the visitor and their residents give
every indication that they are working
for the welfare of the community in
which they live. Granolithic sidewalks
run for thousands of feet in Emigsville
and Mount Wolf. and then, too, the
men are put to work on the streets
scraping and getting them in good
condition for the summer travel. In
Mount Wolf at the present time drag
is being used and it will help in re-
pairing every street in the town.


OF the two towns, Mount Wolf is the
largest and has four industrial plants
10 its credit. Emigsville has only one
industry, a wagon works, where two
score of Acme wagons are manufac-
tured daily.


Making Wire Fabrics


The American Wire Fabrics Com
pany is the largest industry in Mount
Wolf and employment is given to about
zoo men. Wire cloth and screen Is
made by the thousand yards and in
turning out the product almost three
hundred looms are in operation. The
plant was established here about
twelve years ago and at that time only
few men were employed. The bust
ness grew and during the past few
years several new buildings have been
erected and the output greatly in
creased. The main office of the fabric
company is in Chicago and branch fac
tories are located in Clinton, Iowa, and
Niles. Mich.


Another important plant in the town
is operated by the Mount Wolf Furni-
ture Company, of which Henry Wolf is
president and !. Park Wogan is man
ager. In this large plant dining-room
furniture of all descriptions is manu-
factured and many pieces are sold by
furniture dealers in Harrisburg. Tables,
chairs buffets and china closets are
included in the factory's output. At
the present time 125 men are en-

Washington, D. C., Sept. 5.—Showing its complete contempt for the new tariff commission which it maintains, the Democratic party last eliminated the permanent appropriation for the existence of the commission, refused to raise the salary of the commissioners to the original figure of $4,000 a year, and went to the country on its free trade policies.

The Senate and House conference committee on the revenue bill agreed to throw out the continuing appropriation for the commission, designed to make it permanent.

Increases Income Taxes

The revenue bill as passed increases the income taxes, imposes inheritance taxes, provides a protective duty on dyestuffs, taxes profits on munitions, creates a bipartisan tariff commission, changes the wine schedule of the Underwood tariff law, provides measures to prevent the dumping of European products in America after the war at prices with which Americans cannot compete, changes the duties on print paper, continues number of the special emergency taxes which were to expire by limitation on December 31, including taxes on brokers, ship brokers, custom house brokers, theaters and places of amusement, circuses, bowling alleys and billiard tables and manufacturers of tobacco, cigars and cigarettes, and gives the President authority to adopt retaliatory measures toward any belligerent nation that illegally interferes with the trade or commerce of the United States.

The bill was brought before both houses of Congress after a three days conference of a joint committee appointed to harmonize the many points to cut out all stamp taxes, thereby reducing the estimated revenue bill about $5,000,000.

The Tax on Munitions

In order to recoup the reduction in revenue made by abolishing the stamp taxes, the tax on munitions of war was increased from 10 per cent. to 12 1/2 per cent. This provision applies to all manufactures of gunpowder and other explosives except where used for industrial purposes and sporting uses, all projectiles, firearms of every kind used for military purposes, electric motorboats and submarines, or parts of any of these articles. This section of the law is to be imperative within one year after the close of the war in Europe.

A modification of the special tax on joint stock companies and corporations was agreed on by the conferees by which, as the bill becomes a law, there is imposed a tax of so cents for each $1,000 of such stock, with a proviso that the tax shall be based on the fair value of the stock, and in arriving at the estimate of this value surplus and undivided profits shall be taken into account. An exemption amounting to $50,000 is allowed from the capital, surplus and undivided profits before this tax begins to run.

The income tax applies as the bill provides $5,000 in the case of unmarried persons and $4,000 in the case of married man whose wife lives with him, or a married woman whose husband lives with her, as in the present law, but increases from 1 to per cent per annum the tax to be levied, assessed and collected on such net incomes.

The Graduated Income Tax

An additional tax of 1 per cent. per annum is to be levied on the amount by which such net income exceeds $5,000 and does not exceed $10,000; 2 per cent. on the amount by which such net incomes exceed $10,000 and do not exceed $40,000; 3 per cent. between $40,000 and $100,000; 4 per cent. between $100,000 and $150,000; 5 per cent. between $150,000 and $250,000; 6 per cent. between $250,000 and $500,000; 7 per cent. between $500,000 and $1,000,000; 8 per cent. between $1,000,000 and $1,250,000; 9 per cent. between $1,250,000 and $1,500,000; 10 per cent. between $1,500,000 and $2,000,000; 11 per cent. between $2,000,000 and $2,500,000; 12 per cent. between $2,500,000 and $3,000,000, and 13 per cent. on incomes above $3,000,000 per annum.

The members of the Baptist Sunday school held their picnic on the grounds around the church Saturday afternoon with good attendance. Austin Matthews of Westerly was a weekend guest of friends in Palmer town.

Harold Hatchkiss has been spending a few days with New Haven relatives.

The marriage of Miss Lucy Keefe and John McArdle will take place next month at St. Mary's Star of the Sea church, New London. The Ladies' Aid society of the Baptist church served a succotash dinner on the lawn Wednesday noon.

Mr. and Mrs. George Q. Allen of Gay Hill spent this week with Mr. Allen's sister, Mrs. George W. Dart, at her cottage on Mason's Island.

A cottage prayer meeting was held at the home of Mr. and Mrs. Ralph H. Melcer on Tuesday evening.

A number of people from the town attended Hamburg fair.

Work on rebuilding the Palmer Memorial school building is progressing and it is hoped that it will be ready for occupancy by the time the winter term of school begins.

A special service will be held at the Methodist church Sunday afternoon, Sept. 24th, at which Rev. A. W. Newhan superintendent of the Jesse Lee home, Alaska, will give an address.

A social and dance will be held in Tooker's hall Friday night.

following statement which shows determination that wins out: "There

county made in spite of the boil weevil
conditions, as I expect to knock them
out on the first round."


Good for young Thomas. We believe
every word of what he says, too, for
he grew the most corn on an acre this
year in the county and fed a pig
that won first prize at the State Fair
in Macon in her class. Next year he
will have three acres in his crop instead of one. One acre will be put in
corn, one in cotton to be grown in
spite of Mr. Weevil, and one in oats to
be followed with peas. He has already
lined up with Demonstration W. J.
Boyett and says the boy who wins that
Central of Georgia railroad bell next
year will have to do some hustling.

letter gives him these words of encouragement:

note with pleasure that at least one
acre of cotton will be made in spite of
weevils next year. Now you are right,
just stick to your determination next
spring and get every old weevil as
fast as they come out from winter
quarters into your cotton patch, and

square once a week until the middle
of July and I am sure you will be successful in knocking the rascal out all

W. G. OLIVER,


Field Agent in Weevil Work

Russia was presumed to be strictly limited as to material and possessed of an unlimited supply OF men. A description of the alfalfa weevil

In order that farmers in those sec

the bulletin already mentioned con-

early July and may be found by sweep

The adult insect is an oval, brown

Four thousand miles from New York as a telephone message travels, Frank A. Vanderlip, president of the National City Bank, spoke last evening to five hundred members of the Chamber of Commerce of the Borough of Queens in the grand ballroom of the Waldorf Astoria. The occasion was the fifth annual dinner of the association.

Mr. Vanderlip spoke into telephone in Los Angeles, Cal., as each diner listened with a receiver at his ear. Over the wire, following his address, they heard "The Star-Spangled Banner" played in San Francisco, and the roar of the Pacific Ocean at the Golden Gate.

Mayor Mitchell, George Perkins, George A. McAneny, Maurice Z. Connolly, President of the Borough of Queens; Public Service Commissioner Henry Hodge; Frederick Z. Crane, Justice of the Supreme Court, Representative Charles Pope Caldwell, George B. Cortelyou, and Robert Y. Lynch, vice-president of the San Francisco Chamber of Commerce, were the speakers present. Charles G. N. Thomas, president of the Queens Chamber of Commerce, was toastmaster.

"Business Conditions in the United States After the Termination of the European War" was the subject of Mr. Vanderlip's fifteen-minute address.

"Conditions," said the speaker, "may depend partly upon the terms of the peace treaties. They will depend more largely upon the manner in which our own country adjusts itself to the changed international conditions at the close of the war.

In the future we can no longer be provincial. We will be more and more affected by the political status of other nations. In commercial warfare, no matter how much we may desire to, we cannot remain neutral. I believe we are to-day subject to too much law. That we can compete, and compete with a considerable measure of success, with other nations, I firmly believe only if we are not hampered by too many and unwise laws. The serious attention of wise men to this important matter can bring the needed relief."

His objections, the Mayor said, were that the railway refused to allow the city its just returns.

The people of the country must be aroused to realize that sentiment is not enough, but service is required.
